4                             II.  ANALYSIS                                   
5   A.   Legal Standards                                                      
6        In evaluating a motion to dismiss under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6), a court 
7   examines the complaint to determine whether, if the facts alleged are true, plaintiff has stated “a 
8   claim to relief that is plausible on its face.”  Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (quoting 
9   Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007)).  A claim is plausible if plaintiff has pleaded 
10   “factual content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable 
11   for the misconduct alleged.”  Id.  “Threadbare recitals of the elements of a cause of action, 
12   supported by mere conclusory statements, do not suffice” (id.), nor do “allegations that are merely 

13   conclusory, unwarranted deductions of fact, or unreasonable inferences.”  Sprewell v. Golden State 
14   Warriors, 266 F.3d 979, 988 (9th Cir. 2001).  “If a motion to dismiss is granted, a court should 
15   normally grant leave to amend unless it determines that the pleading could not possibly be cured 
16   by allegations of other facts.”  Chinatown Neighborhood Ass’n v. Harris, 33 F. Supp. 3d 1085, 
17   1093 (N.D. Cal. 2014).                                                    
18        A heightened pleading standard under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 9(b) applies to 
19   allegations of fraudulent conduct when fraud is an essential element of the claim or the claim is 
20   “grounded in” fraudulent conduct.  Vess v. Ciba-Geigy Corp. USA, 317 F.3d 1097, 1103–04 (9th 
21   Cir. 2003).  Under Rule 9(b), “[i]n alleging fraud or mistake, a party must state with particularity 
22   the circumstances constituting fraud or mistake.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 9(b).  The fraud allegations “must 

23   be specific enough to give defendants notice of the particular misconduct which is alleged to 
24   constitute the fraud charged so that they can defend against the charge and not just deny that they 
1   have done anything wrong.”  In re Finjan Holdings, Inc., 58 F.4th 1048, 1057 (9th Cir. 2023) 
2   (quoting Bly-Magee v. California, 236 F.3d 1014, 1019 (9th Cir. 2001)).  To meet this standard, a 
3   plaintiff’s “[a]verments of fraud must be accompanied by ‘the who, what, when, where, and how’ 

4   of the misconduct charged.”  Vess, 317 F.3d at 1106 (quoting Cooper v. Pickett, 137 F.3d 616, 627 
5   (9th Cir. 1997)).  The allegation “must set forth what is false or misleading about a statement, and 
6   why it is false.”  Id. (quoting In re GlenFed, Inc. Sec. Litig., 42 F.3d 1541, 1548 (9th Cir. 1994)).

12   C.   The Complaint Fails to Allege RICO Claims Based on Other Acts with Particularity. 

13        The complaint lists multiple claims for violation of the RICO Act, 18 U.S.C. § 1962.  
14   Section 1962(a) prohibits any person from using money derived from a pattern of racketeering 
15   activity to invest in an enterprise, Section 1962(b) prohibits any person from gaining control of an 
16   enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity, and Section 1962(c) prohibits any person from 
17   conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity.  18 U.S.C. § 1962.  Section 
18   1962(d) prohibits a person from conspiring to violate Sections 1962(a)–(c).  Id.  Thus, an element 
19   of each of these claims is “racketeering activity,” which is defined to include mail fraud, wire 
20   fraud, and bank fraud, among other conduct.  See 18 U.S.C. § 1961(1).     
21        To state a claim for violation of Section 1962(a), a plaintiff must plausibly allege that a 
22   person  received  money  from  a  pattern  of  racketeering  activity,  invested  those  racketeering 

23   proceeds, and that plaintiff was “injured by ‘the use or investment of racketeering income,’ as 
24   opposed to the racketeering activity itself.”  De Los Angeles Gomez v. Bank of Am., N.A., 642 F. 
1   App’x 670, 675 (9th Cir. 2016) (quoting Nugget Hydroelectric, L.P. v. Pac. Gas & Elec. Co., 981 
2   F.2d 429, 437 (9th Cir. 1992)).  “[A plaintiff] must allege that the investment of racketeering 
3   income was the proximate cause of its injury.  Reinvestment of proceeds from alleged racketeering 

4   activity back into the enterprise to continue its racketeering activity is insufficient to show 
5   proximate causation.”  Sybersound Records, Inc. v. UAV Corp., 517 F.3d 1137, 1149 (9th Cir. 
6   2008).                                                                    
7        To state a violation of Section 1962(b), a plaintiff must plausibly allege facts that explain 
8   how each defendant gained control of a RICO enterprise through racketeering activity, and how it 
9   “suffered a distinct injury” from each defendant’s purported control of the enterprise.  De Los 
10   Angeles Gomez, 642 F. App’x at 675.                                       
11        “To state a civil claim for violations of [Section] 1962(c), a plaintiff must allege ‘(1) 
12   conduct (2) of an enterprise (3) through a pattern (4) of racketeering activity (known as “predicate 

13   acts”) (5) causing injury to plaintiff’s business or property.’”  United Energy Trading, LLC v. Pac. 
14   Gas & Elec. Co., 146 F. Supp. 3d 1122, 1138 (N.D. Cal. 2015) (quoting Grimmett v. Brown, 75 
15   F.3d 506, 510 (9th Cir. 1996)).                                           
16        And to state a claim for violation of Section 1962(d), the plaintiff must allege facts showing 
17   that the defendant “was aware of the essential nature and scope of the enterprise and intended to 
18   participate in it.”  Baumer v. Pachl, 8 F.3d 1341, 1346 (9th Cir. 1993) (quoting United States v. 
19   Muskovsky, 863 F.2d 1319, 1324 (7th Cir. 1988)).

6        In evaluating a motion to dismiss under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6), a court 
7   examines the complaint to determine whether, if the facts alleged are true, plaintiff has stated “a 
8   claim to relief that is plausible on its face.”  Ashcroft v. Iqbal,
556 U.S. 662, 678
 (2009) (quoting 
9   Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly,
550 U.S. 544, 570
 (2007)).  A claim is plausible if plaintiff has pleaded 
10   “factual content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable 
11   for the misconduct alleged.”
Id.
  “Threadbare recitals of the elements of a cause of action, 
12   supported by mere conclusory statements, do not suffice” (id.), nor do “allegations that are merely 

13   conclusory, unwarranted deductions of fact, or unreasonable inferences.”  Sprewell v. Golden State 
14   Warriors,
266 F.3d 979, 988
 (9th Cir. 2001).  “If a motion to dismiss is granted, a court should 
15   normally grant leave to amend unless it determines that the pleading could not possibly be cured 
16   by allegations of other facts.”  Chinatown Neighborhood Ass’n v. Harris,
33 F. Supp. 3d 1085
, 
17   1093 (N.D. Cal. 2014).                                                    
18        A heightened pleading standard under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 9(b) applies to 
19   allegations of fraudulent conduct when fraud is an essential element of the claim or the claim is 
20   “grounded in” fraudulent conduct.  Vess v. Ciba-Geigy Corp. USA,
317 F.3d 1097
, 1103–04 (9th 
21   Cir. 2003).  Under Rule 9(b), “[i]n alleging fraud or mistake, a party must state with particularity 
22   the circumstances constituting fraud or mistake.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 9(b).  The fraud allegations “must 

23   be specific enough to give defendants notice of the particular misconduct which is alleged to 
24   constitute the fraud charged so that they can defend against the charge and not just deny that they 
1   have done anything wrong.”  In re Finjan Holdings, Inc.,
58 F.4th 1048, 1057
 (9th Cir. 2023) 
2   (quoting Bly-Magee v. California,
236 F.3d 1014, 1019
 (9th Cir. 2001)).  To meet this standard, a 
3   plaintiff’s “[a]verments of fraud must be accompanied by ‘the who, what, when, where, and how’ 

4   of the misconduct charged.”  Vess,
317 F.3d at 1106
 (quoting Cooper v. Pickett,
137 F.3d 616
, 627
